content: The study was a randomized, open-label, phase 3 non-inferiority trial designed to compare the efficacy and safety of a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid (1-month group) with 9 months of isoniazid monotherapy (9-month group) in HIV-infected patients. These patients either lived in areas with high tuberculosis (TB) prevalence or had evidence of latent TB infection. The primary endpoint was the first diagnosis of TB or death due to TB or an unknown cause. Approximately 80% of participants did not have bacteriologically confirmed TB. Enrollment was restricted to individuals aged 13 years or older who were not pregnant or breastfeeding. The overall TB incidence observed in the trial was lower than expected. The number of patients with a CD4+ count below 250 cells per cubic millimeter was small, and the study did not demonstrate either inferiority or non-inferiority of the 1-month regimen in this subgroup. Deaths of unknown cause were censored in the analysis, which could introduce bias in the incidence rate difference if some of these deaths were related to TB. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) downgraded the quality of evidence by one level due to the open-label design, which could lead to performance bias. However, the quality was not downgraded for indirectness, even though the trial compared 1HP with 9H and did not include other regimens like 6H, which is a widely used standard of care in TB preventive treatment (TPT). The GDG also noted that inconsistency could not be assessed because only a single trial was available, and additional trials would be desirable. The trial was conducted exclusively in people living with HIV (PLHIV) and not in all individuals at risk of active TB. Probable TB diagnoses and deaths without bacteriological confirmation were censored at the time of the event. When the cause of death was determined to be unknown or unrelated to TB by blinded external reviewers, these were treated as competing risks rather than endpoints. However, some of these deaths might have been due to TB, potentially biasing the estimates. In the 1-month arm, there were 21 deaths, 3 of which were related to TB. In the 9-month arm, there were 28 deaths, 3 of which were related to TB. Deaths were reviewed by blinded external reviewers, and unknown causes of death were included as endpoints, but misclassification of the cause of death could bias the estimates. The trial also assessed adherence via participant self-report during clinic visits. Resistance may have been non-emergent and derived from the infecting strain. A small sample of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases had drug susceptibility test results available. The GDG noted that although one of the trials was conducted in low TB incidence countries, this was unlikely to affect the relative effect of rifapentine plus isoniazid compared with isoniazid monotherapy. The quality of evidence was not downgraded for this reason. However, the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for both relative and absolute effects included appreciable benefit and harm with the 3HP regimen. The open-label design of the trials may have introduced bias in the ascertainment of adverse events. Very low event rates were observed, and the upper limit of the 95% CI for both relative and absolute effects included appreciable harm with 3HP, leading to a downgrade by two levels. In children and adolescents, the trial comparing 3-month weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid with 6 or 9 months of isoniazid monotherapy showed moderate overall quality of evidence. The GDG downgraded the evidence by one level due to the open-label design, which could introduce ascertainment bias. The results met the pre-stated non-inferiority margin, and the quality was not downgraded for imprecision despite the small number of events. In pregnant and postpartum women, isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) was compared to no IPT or placebo. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low due to serious bias from confounding and measurement issues. Liver function tests were only performed when clinically indicated, which could have been influenced by knowledge of IPT receipt, introducing bias in the assessment of hepatotoxicity. For individuals in contact with patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), two randomized controlled trials (TB CHAMP in South Africa and VQUIN in Vietnam) evaluated 6 months of levofloxacin. The pooled analysis of individual participant data was used to estimate effects. The GDG downgraded the evidence by one level for imprecision due to small sample sizes and zero events in some cases. Additionally, indirectness was noted as a limitation since data were only available for individuals aged over 15 years in the VQUIN trial.
